implementation_notes: The routing decision is a route definition: ordered when() predicates are evaluated per Exchange and the first match wins, otherwise() handles the default, and precondition() freezes the branch at startup so a property-driven routing table costs nothing per message. Choose it when Camel is already the integration layer, because the rule set stays declarative and the DSL is the pattern's own EIP implementation; note that route changes are a redeploy.
pitfalls: Predicates read the mutable Exchange, so an earlier processor can change the routing outcome.
Nested EIPs need end()/endChoice() or the route graph is built with the wrong scope.

variants.name: Spring Integration router (annotation or XML)
variants.idiom_name: @Router method returning a channel name / PayloadTypeRouter / HeaderValueRouter
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Integration models the router as a first-class endpoint: a @Router method (or a HeaderValue/PayloadType/RecipientList router bean) returns the resolved channel name, resolution-required defaults to true so an unresolved message raises MessageDeliveryException rather than disappearing, and default-output-channel is the explicit else branch. Choose it when the application is already a Spring Integration flow and routing must live with the other endpoints; the routing class is a plain Spring bean, so it is easy to unit-test.
pitfalls: resolution-required=true makes an unroutable message an exception - deliberate, but it must be handled or it pollutes the error channel.
Channel resolution failures are only as visible as the error channel's subscribers; without one they are logs nobody reads.
